item.title: Go under Chinese Rules with a Succinct Game History is Complete for Exponential Space
item.description: arXiv:2611.18201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The complexity of games is a central topic in combinatorics, algorithms, and computational complexity theory. It asks how difficult it is to determine the winner of a combinatorial game under optimal play. Many games, such as Hex or Othello, are PSPACE-complete: the game tree has polynomial depth, so the game can be decided in PSPACE. However, some games allow exponentially long plays, for instance Chess (without a generalized 50-move rule) or Go under Japanese rules; these are complete for exponential time. To prevent infinite games, some games employ a no-repetition rule (super-ko rule), for instance Go under Chinese rules. Robson (1984) proved that Chess and Checkers with a no-repetition rule are even harder: deciding whether the first player has a winning strategy is EXPSPACE-complete. Since then, it has been an open problem whether Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete, too. The complexity of a game under a no-repetition rule is typically interpreted as follows: given a board position, decide whether the first player has a winning strategy such that no repetition occurs from that position on. We introduce the concept of a succinct game history: a Boolean circuit that, given a board position, outputs 1 if the position is in the game history and 0 otherwise. It serves as a "judge" that tells the players whether a move is illegal because it creates a repetition. We prove that deciding whether Black has a winning strategy in Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete when the game history is given succinctly. Moreover, the starting position in our hardness proof is reachable by legal gameplay, which has not always been the case in prior proofs.
item.dc:creator: Markus Bl\"aser, Felix Czerner

item.title: Disenfranchisement in Spatial Voting Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.18468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion. In order to understand how ideological or issue diversity may impact the stability of such inclusion and exclusion, we introduce franchise elections, where voting members of a group vote to change the electorate. In particular, when agents are positioned inside an ideological or issue space, a social choice function that aggregates agent viewpoints induces a preference for agents over group composition, where agents prefer groups that improve the social choice function outcome for them. We demonstrate that when ideological space is two-dimensional, these franchise elections can generate complex behavior and that this complexity exists for any social choice function. Using the Yolk social choice function from voting theory, we illustrate that franchise elections can predict that agents attempting to introduce a new ideological axis perpendicular to an existing left-right spectrum risk disenfranchisement unless they ally with either side of the spectrum, and that franchise elections can cycle with any period.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Lageschulte, Joel Nishimura

item.title: Stochastic Games with Distributional Entropy Objectives
item.description: arXiv:2611.18470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce \emph{stochastic games with distributional entropy objectives}, two-player zero-sum games whose configurations are probability distributions over the states of a finite arena and whose stage reward is Shannon entropy. Over an infinite discounted horizon, MIN seeks to concentrate the distribution, while MAX seeks to disperse it. Because entropy is nonlinear, it matters whether strategic and transition randomness are averaged before entropy is evaluated or sampled first. We formalise three resulting semantics: averaged-distribution, sampled-profile, and sampled-transition. This semantic choice fundamentally changes the game-theoretic structure. Averaged-distribution games need not be determined, even on a four-state deterministic arena, whereas both sampled semantics are determined and admit optimal stationary randomised strategies. We give contractive Bellman characterisations and convergent finite-horizon approximations for the upper and lower averaged values and the two sampled values. Moreover, even the lower value under averaged-distribution semantics dominates the value under either sampled semantics, while the sampled-profile and sampled-transition values are incomparable in general. For fixed rational discount and positive rational promise gap, the averaged-distribution (upper and lower value) gap problems and both sampled gap problems lie in PSPACE; for a single entropy minimiser, the averaged and sampled-profile problems lie in NP. Finally, under all three semantics, entropy optimisation is NP-hard to approximate within a suitable fixed additive constant, already for deterministic one-player games, where pure memoryless strategies are optimal.
item.dc:creator: Shankaranarayanan Krishna, Durgam Latha, Dion Reji, Ashutosh Trivedi

item.title: Online Fair Division Meets Reordering Buffers
item.description: arXiv:2607.01159v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the online fair division of indivisible mixed manna among agents with additive valuation functions. Under the standard online model, at each time step an indivisible item arrives; each agent may assign it a positive, negative, or zero value, and it must be irrevocably allocated, before the arrival of the next item. At the same time, we also wish to maintain some fairness guarantee, and in this work we focus on envy-freeness (EF) and one of its most prominent relaxations, envy-freeness up to one item (EF1). Given the strong negative and the scarce positive results for this problem without additional assumptions, we augment our algorithms with buffers that can store and rearrange a limited number of items. This setting interpolates naturally between the fully online case (no buffer) and the fully offline case (a buffer large enough to hold all items). We show that algorithms equipped with reasonably sized buffers can achieve strong guarantees for personalized $k$-value instances, i.e., instances in which each agent assigns at most $k$ distinct values to items. In particular, we construct allocations that are EF1 at every time step and EF at most time steps, using a buffer of size linear in $k$ and in the number of agents. Our approach relies on novel combinatorial arguments and on constructing a sequence of envy-free matchings that allocates most items. Finally, we extend our results to general additive valuation functions, with a dependence on the largest per-agent ratio between two values of the same sign, and we also identify limitations of our approach via impossibility results on the use of buffers with smaller size.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Amanatidis, Giulio Giaconi, Evangelos Markakis, Nicos Protopapas

item.title: Designing Information in a Forest: Algorithmic Aspects
item.description: arXiv:2611.16327v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Bayesian persuasion framework models strategic information revelation by a sender to one or more receivers. We study an intricate version of the multi-receiver persuasion setting in which the communication hierarchy is a forest - i.e., some receivers observe more informative signals than others, and the partial ordering of the receivers according to the information they get is represented by a pre-specified directed forest. This model naturally captures interactions in hierarchical organizations, and it lies in between the two most commonly studied versions of Bayesian persuasion: private persuasion and public persuasion. Inspired by the classic model of private persuasion, we focus on a setting with a binary state of nature and binary-action heterogeneous receivers s.t. the sender's utility is a monotone function of the set of receivers taking a specific desirable action. We extend the computational tractability result for symmetric sender's utility from private persuasion to the forest hierarchy framework using methodology inspired by optimal transport theory. We further provide a polynomial-time algorithm when the sender's utility is modular. On the negative side, we show that, unlike in private persuasion, the case of a supermodular sender's utility function leads to an NP-hard optimization problem which further does not admit an FPTAS unless P=NP; this result holds even when each tree component of the forest is a chain of 3 receivers. To complement the hardness result, we provide a simple approximation algorithm with the approximation ratio depending linearly on the depth of the forest hierarchy. We further provide an analogous algorithm for the submodular utility case. Finally, beyond forest communication hierarchies, we rule out an FPTAS for the sender's optimal utility even in the symmetric utility case, unless P=NP.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Zabarnyi

item.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
item.description: arXiv:2611.17148v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.
item.dc:creator: Mark Lovett, Feng Fu

item.title: Games with $\omega$-Automatic Preference Relations
item.description: arXiv:2503.04759v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper investigates Nash equilibria (NEs) in multi-player turn-based games on graphs, where player preferences are modeled as $\omega$-automatic relations via deterministic parity automata. Unlike much of the existing literature, which focuses on specific reward functions, our results apply to any preference relation definable by an $\omega$-automatic relation. We analyze the computational complexity of determining the existence of an NE (possibly under some constraints), verifying whether a given strategy profile forms an NE, and checking whether a specific outcome can be realized by an NE. When a (constrained) NE exists, we show that there always exists one with finite-memory strategies. Finally, we explore fundamental properties of $\omega$-automatic relations and their implications for the existence of equilibria.
item.dc:creator: V\'eronique Bruy\`ere, Christophe Grandmont, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Raskin

item.title: Faster Symmetric Rendezvous on Four or More Locations
item.description: arXiv:2604.02058v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the symmetric rendezvous problem, two players follow the same (randomized) strategy to visit one of $n$ locations in each time step $t=0,1,2,\dots$. Their goal is to minimize the expected time until they visit the same location and thus meet. A canonical strategy due to Anderson and Weber (J. Appl. Probab., 1990) is known to be optimal for $n=2$ and $n=3$ (Weber, Math. Oper. Res. 2012), but whether it remains optimal for larger values of $n$ has been an open question since 1990. We show that it does not remain optimal: for any finite $n\geq 4$, we construct an explicit symmetric strategy that achieves a strictly smaller expected meeting time than the Anderson-Weber strategy. In the Anderson-Weber strategy players stay at a dedicated home location for $n-1$ steps with a certain probability $\theta$ and with the remaining probability tour all non-home locations in a random order. Our improving strategy introduces carefully chosen correlations between consecutive tours of the non-home locations. The construction is uniform in $n$ and is guided by a graph-theoretic view in which tours correspond to permutations and meetings to edges in the complement of the derangement graph. By exploiting the clique structure of this graph we obtain a correlated strategy that improves on the Anderson-Weber strategy. For $n=4$, we give an exact expression for the improvement; for any $n\geq 5$, we obtain a lower bound on the expected improvement of $\frac{483(1-\theta)^6}{(n-1)^8}$, where $\theta \in [0,1)$ is the probability of staying at the home location. The graph-theoretic framework we introduce may be useful more widely in the design and analysis of correlated strategies for rendezvous.
item.dc:creator: Javier Cembrano, Felix Fischer, Max Klimm

item.title: Dynamic Pooling and Regional Participation in Deceased-Donor Organ Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2609.18147v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Moving from geographically fragmented to pooled waiting lists in deceased-donor organ transplantation can improve efficiency, but it raises concerns about regional fairness and participation incentives. This paper studies Pareto gains from such transitions in a multiclass queueing model with impatient agents, perishable items, and a tractable homogeneous compatibility friction. In contrast to standard approaches that emphasize static match quality or overlook regional incentives in dynamic contexts, this analysis identifies dynamic risk pooling as the primary source of Pareto improvements for regions. Pooling reduces organ waste resulting from stochastic supply-demand fluctuations, temporal mismatches, and random compatibility outcomes. Although this dynamic surplus theoretically enables Pareto improvements, a purely utilitarian policy that treats all patients equally across regions often fails to achieve these improvements when regions are asymmetric. In these situations, utilitarian redistribution removes an excessive number of organs from high-supply regions and violates their participation constraints. To address this conflict, it is demonstrated that the set of achievable utilities can be represented by mixtures of static priority index policies. Building on this structure, the Constrained Pareto Frontier Search (CPFS) is proposed as a polynomial-time procedure that computes an approximately optimal allocation policy with arbitrarily small participation-constraint violations, implemented as a single priority list with a lottery at registration. The results indicate that, by adjusting priority indices to ensure redistribution remains within the gains from pooled supply, demand, and compatibility risk, policymakers can achieve global efficiency while maintaining local participation incentives.
item.dc:creator: Genta Okada

item.title: Some complete $\omega$-powers of a one-counter language in the difference hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2610.16473v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fix a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ having at least two letters, and natural numbers $n,k\geq 1$. We denote by $D_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$ the class of differences of $n$ subsets of the Cantor space $\Sigma^\omega$ in $\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k$, and by $D^-_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$ the class of complements of sets in $D_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$. We prove, for any natural numbers $n,k\geq 1$, the existence of a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ having at least two letters and a finitary language $U_{n,k}$ over $\Sigma$ accepted by a one-counter automaton such that the $\omega$-power $$U_{n,k}^\infty:=\{ w_0w_1\cdots\in\Sigma^\omega\mid\forall i\in\omega ~~w_i\in U_{n,k}\}$$ is $D_{2n-1}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$-complete. We also prove a conditional result for the dual classes $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$: under the assumption that there exists a finitary language $V_{n,3}$ accepted by a one-counter automaton, such that its $\omega$-power $V_{n,3}^\infty$ is $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_3)$-complete, there would also exist, for any integer $k > 3$, a finitary language $V_{n,k}$ accepted by a one-counter automaton, such that its $\omega$-power $V_{n,k}^\infty$ is $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$-complete. Finally we add another conditionnal result about Wadge degrees of rational $\mathbf{\Delta}^0_2$ omega powers, which completes the recent results of [FGL26].
item.dc:creator: Jacques Duparc (UNIL), Olivier Finkel (IMJ-PRG), Dominique Lecomte (IMJ-PRG)

item.title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.14182v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Maresch, Erik Schulze, Jnan Yalla
